utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Good morning, everybody. Madam Registrar, good morning to you. Could you be kind enough to call the case, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. This is the case number IT-05-88-T, the Prosecutor versus Vujadin Popovic et al.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you, ma'am. All the accused are here. Defence teams, I only note the absence of Madam Nikolic and Mr. Haynes and Ms. Condon. The Prosecution is Mr. McCloskey, Mr. Nicholls and Mr. Thayer. Anyone else? No. Witness is present. Good morning to you, General.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. Welcome back. Let's hope we'll finish with the testimony as early as possible so that you can go home. Mr. McCloskey. How much more time do you require?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: I just have three or four documents. I think we should get it done hopefully in 20 minutes if we don't get into any real long discussions. Good morning, everyone.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Good morning, General. I think we remember your answer yesterday when were you asked about General Gvero and his responsibility or his potential dealings with prisoners. Who would be the primary assistant commander that may be dealing with prisoners of war issues?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Josse?

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: We are a little unclear as to whether Mr. McCloskey meant General Gvero there. If he did, then fair enough.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: I was asking about which assistant commander would be dealing mostly with prisoners. He'd said that it wasn't Gvero's primary concern and so I was asking who would it have been.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Thank you. I think I'm being oversensitive.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you. No. I would have done exactly the same, Mr. Josse.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: I'm sorry I didn't quote what he said but my recollection was that it wasn't --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Go ahead, go ahead.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: General, I think you can answer the question if you understood it. I know we sometimes confuse things but we are not meaning to.

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In the organisation of the army of Republika Srpska or the corps or commands, there is no person or a team designated to work with prisoners of war. Prisoners of war are interviewed and interrogated by the intelligence and security organs. As for the accommodation of prisoners of war, and providing for their security, the concern for the respect of international conventions with respect to the prisoners of war is in the hands of the administration for logistics. That is also in charge of setting up prisoner of war camps.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Do the military police have -- usually have responsibility for prisoners of war on the brigade level?

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And are they overseen by the chief of security, generally, related to issues of prisoners of war?

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: When it comes to the use of the military police, the person in charge is the security organ, regardless of the issue, be it the prisoners of war, escorting convoys or any other police task.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right. If we could go to a document that mentions prisoners of war, it's number 131, and I've got a -- we have a -- both a teletype version and a handwritten version, originals, which I think it would be easier, General, if you took a look at both of them. I think the teletype may come up on the screen but if I could get some help from the usher, I'll let you take a look at them. You can see it on the screen. It's a pretty good copy. But there is also -- let me hand you the originals. The screen, there is also a handwritten version which is the page -- which is page 2, if we could flip to that so that everyone can see the handwritten version. And if you could, General, if you could look at the original handwritten version to your right, and it's in Cyrillic, do you recognise that handwriting by any chance? I know it's been a long time.

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not familiar with the handwriting. I can only see that the assistant commander, General Major Z Tolimir is indicated down here.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay. Well, Let's go back to the typed version so you can concentrate on that and you have the original in front of you, which is page 1. This is a document that we see that's from the command of the 1st Podrinje Light Infantry Brigade which we know to be Rogatica, dated 13 July, from the -- and it says, to VRS, Main Staff, to General Gvero personally and it's entitled "Accommodation of R/Z." What does R/Z mean?

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Prisoners of war.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay. And this talks about accommodating prisoners of war from Srebrenica, and I won't go over all of it but it talks about using them for agricultural work. And it says it would be best if this new group, which has not been in contact with the other prisoners of war. First of all, this is the 13th, I think you were in the Krajina, so do you know anything about this agricultural work and Rogatica, prisoners, anything like that?

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The month of July is not the time of harvest. The region is mountainous so I really don't know what agricultural work could that refer to. I only know that there is a horse farm between Rogatica and Sokolac. That's the only thing that comes to mind. Apart from that, I really wouldn't know what agricultural work could be referred to.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay. And can you tell us anything about -- we see that it's addressed to General Gvero personally at the Main Staff, from Tolimir. Can you -- and I don't want to you speculate but can you -- what can you tell us about why General Gvero would be receiving this information personally?

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Probably, I think, because at that time General Gvero was the oldest officer, the oldest general, in the Main Staff. Yesterday we looked at a document where it says that General Tolimir was sent mail to the forward command post of the Drina Corps, and now the document is sent to the Main Staff addressed to General Gvero probably because Gvero must have been the oldest general at the command post. That's the only explanation I can give you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right. Now, the translation said oldest general. I don't think age makes a difference.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Don't lead. Just ask, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. McCloskey.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Can you tell us whether or not you meant to say oldest or did you-- was there a translation issue?

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The most senior by function, and by rank.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you. All right. Let me go to another document. This is 65 ter number 36. You may have had a chance to see that, and I've got a hard copy, if that's easier for you because it is a -- it is a two-page document. And this is a document, again Main Staff, from the Main Staff, dated 13 July, it's very urgent to the commands of the Drina Corps and several Drina Corps brigades that we recognise, and it's entitled, "Order to prevent the passage of Muslim groups toward Tuzla and Kladanj." And it's entitled, "An order" and I won't go over all the order. I think you can take a look at it. I don't know -- have you -- have you seen this document before, General?

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I haven't.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Well, feel free to take a look at it so that I can ask you a couple of questions about it, and I'm not really -- I'm not going to go into the detail of the order. What I'm mostly interested in is the fact that it is an order from the Main Staff and it's -- and it's in the name of assistant commander Lieutenant General Milan Gvero, and what I'm interested in is is there anything unusual about him issuing an order like this in his capacity based on what your earlier description of his duties and the duties of the Main Staff were?

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know -- are you asking me to confirm, deny or provide my opinion?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Provide your opinion on whether or not this would -- this appears to be something that would be done in the normal course or is there something unusual about General Gvero --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Josse?

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: On what basis is my learned friend asking the witness to provide his opinion? As an expert? We suggest that in reality, this is straying into the field of expertise and the Prosecution have never advanced this particular gentleman as an expert.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Well, but the -- this is all prompted by the reply of the witness himself. He said, "I don't know. Are you asking me to confirm, deny or provide my opinion?" And he's being asked then to provide an opinion but I think it's the opinion of the witness, not -- there is no indication that he's being asked this question as an expert. Exactly. He was a superior in any case. So I don't see the difficulty.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Can I see the signature before that? I'm not sure that this was signed by General Gvero.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Yes, this is --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I see General Zivanovic at the end.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Well, we may have a computer issue. I apologise about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Of course I was going to come to that later, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Josse.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: We better go to 45. I'm sorry. Thank you, Mr. President. The witness has the correct one but thank you, Your Honour. So let's get that up there and go to the second page to make sure we've got the right one. There we go. Thank you. General, I was -- based on the earlier descriptions you've given in response to Defence counsel about the responsibilities of assistant commanders, their ability to issue orders, can you -- yeah, give us your, as his superior, your opinion of this. Is this -- can this be viewed in the normal course of business or is there something unusual about this?

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The unusual thing is this. This is an executive document of a staff sector which I conclude by the number 03/04, this is the indication of the staff sector. It was signed by assistant commander, I don't see the initial, Lieutenant General Gvero. It all depends on whether the commander of the Main Staff, General Mladic, had previously authorised General Gvero to sign executive orders, because this executive order can be also treated as a combat order. I cannot tell you whether this was done legally or illegally. It would be in keeping with the law if the commander of the Main Staff had authorised General Gvero to issue executive orders and it would be against the law if General Gvero had not previously been authorised to issue them.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Did you ever know General Gvero throughout the war to issue significant combat orders without authorisation from General Mladic?

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Never ever any one of us issued a combat order without special authority by Mladic and I have already told you when this could take place. It could have taken place only if General Mladic sent one of his assistants to a part of the front line and authorised him to command forces in that part of the front line. Like for example he gave me authority to look after Bihac, Lukavac 93, Glamoc, Grahovo. I would have been so much better off if I hadn't been authorised to deal with these front lines.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. One moment, Mr. McCloskey. We -- because I forgot earlier on and I apologise. We are sitting pursuant to 15 bis this morning. Judge Stole can't be with us.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right. General, just a couple more. If we could now go to 65 ter 2754, now we've gone to -- we are going to General Miletic this time, and hopefully the B/C/S will come on to your screen but I'll just slowly give us a background. I have a again it's Main Staff of the army Republika Srpska and it's got that confidential number 03/4-1654, and it's, you can see, to the 1st Krajina Corps and the Drina Corps, for the information of the 1st Zvornik Infantry Brigade, commander or Chief of Staff personally. Now I won't get into this, but I would like you to have a chance to read it so if we could -- thank you. But we can see from this that it has to do with dispatching units to the Zvornik Brigade, and on the 15th of July, which I think is a date 1995 that everyone recognises. And we see at the bottom that General Miletic's name and again standing in for the Chief of Staff. Same general question I had before: Is there anything unusual about this or is this in keeping with the job descriptions and responsibilities that you have told us about General Miletic earlier?

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There is nothing unusual in here. This is not even an order. It is not a directive. This is just information, as far as I can see from the text. Somebody from the Main Staff, I suppose it was the commander himself, had agreed with the commander of the 1st Krajina Corps to assist the 1st Zvornik Brigade by sending an infantry company. In other words, this information was sent both to the 1st Krajina and the Drina Corps and the commander of the Zvornik Brigade was copied so as to let him know that the company will arrive, in keeping with the previous agreement as indicated under number 1 in line 1. This is nothing unusual. And as for the signature standing in for the Chief of Staff, I believe we have already discussed that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Yes. So that's -- that would be -- this kind of work would be the kind of thing that you would have expected him to stand in for you with? Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. This is information. Under item 4, it says here the orientation time, 1400 hours, the arrival of the company, around 2000 hours. This is just a warning to the brigade commander, I believe that it was Pandurevic, that the company would arrive, that he should provide for their accommodation, and the information was also to the command to -- of the Drina Corps so as to inform them of what was going on in the area of their responsibility.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right. Thank you. The next one I'd like to go to is 65 ter number 191. And this is a 25 July 1995 document in the name of General Tolimir, and it's again from the 1st Podrinje Light Infantry Brigade and it's -- there you can see it, entitled "very urgent" and it's the Main Staff of the Republika Srpska army, personally to General Gvero or Miletic. And before I ask you about your thoughts on that particular address to General Gvero or Miletic, if you could take just a bit of time to read the document. I'm sorry, I don't have the B/C/S, so we'll need to use the screen. As we can see, this appears to regard prisoners and a bit about Zepa and the agreement about the status of prisoners, and if you could take particular attention to paragraph 2, the last -- the last sentence in paragraph 2, we can see that they are talking in paragraph 2 about the Muslims demand that General Gobillard come to Zepa as UNPROFOR representative and representatives of ICRC and it says, "Pass on to UNPROFOR a request to send an officer of colonel rank from Sarajevo sector to UNPROFOR check-point 2 at Boksanica to monitor the execution of the agreement." And what I wanted to ask you about first of all is this paragraph that says, "Make a note to them that we don't want them to send a general, considering that we have information that they want to take advantage of his presence according to similar scenario when they took advantage of the presence of General Morillon in Srebrenica in 1993." Now I think we are all familiar enough with the situation with General Morillon in 1993 that we don't need to talk about that too much. But can you tell us briefly why Tolimir is worried about having a general from the UNPROFOR? And of course you can incorporate 1993 into the answer. I just, as you know, ask you to be as brief as you can.

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I do have to mention General Morillon and year 1993 for the simple reason that at the time General Morillon abused his position as force commander of the UNPROFOR for Bosnia-Herzegovina and entered a Srebrenica that was already under blockade. It was just before the enclave in Srebrenica was created, or the protected area. On so-called yellow land, I was with Morillon. I met with Morillon. And Tolimir was part of that delegation. And he knew all that was going on. So all that Tolimir is doing in this document is invoking his own experience from 1993. I have some sort of original, and it doesn't say exactly, "we demand." It says, "Please remind them not to send officers with the rank of general." I believe it was about an exchange of prisoners. "A colonel will do because we have information that they want to abuse his presence according to the same scenario as they abused the presence of Morillon in Srebrenica in 1993." So this is all about applying some standards of conduct to that situation in 1995.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: So is it your view that it would be easier to control a UNPROFOR colonel than it would be a general like Morillon?

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: An UNPROFOR colonel, whoever he is, would not have the same powers as a general, because the UNPROFOR did not have that many generals, after all. It had a Chief of Staff for Bosnia-Herzegovina, and it had one at the UNPROFOR headquarters, and both of them had greater powers than some colonel who was chief of sector, and that colonel -- sorry -- that general, if he came, he would also have the right to issue orders because Morillon came in February 1993 in Srebrenica with 19 soldiers. He mixed in with Muslim soldiers and even if we had wanted to attack, we couldn't because UNPROFOR served them as a human shield, and that's one of the things that Tolimir must have been afraid of. He thought that Muslims could go back on their agreement, as they did many times before, and they would have a general as protection.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: So just my short question was: Was it -- would it be easier to control a colonel than a general and prevent a colonel from taking advantage like Morillon did, in your words? That's supposed to be a yes or no question but you can always explain it if you can't answer it that way, General. Answer it the way you feel best fit to do so, of course.

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Certainly, it's easier to control a colonel because a colonel has no authority to change an agreement. In this case, an agreement had been reached with the mediation of the UNPROFOR on an exchange of prisoners, but when it is supposed to happen, Muslims can go back on it and say, "We don't want the exchange." If a general of the UNPROFOR were present, he could agree with the Muslims or not. If he does agree, then the whole thing falls through. But a colonel is not in a position either to agree with the Muslims or not. He can in no way influence the initial agreement. So I would choose yes, it is easier to control a colonel than general.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay. And then could we go back to the front page, where I mentioned previously that we see personally to General Gvero or General Miletic, and again can you tell us your view why Tolimir would address it to either of them like that, if you can -- if you think you can answer that?

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The sequence would be Gvero, then Miletic. It's obvious that Tolimir doesn't know which of the two is at the Main Staff, and he's sending this document to the Main Staff to be handed to whomever the messenger finds. But there couldn't be anyone but Gvero and Miletic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you. I've got one more last one. We are about there. This is 65 ter 2517, and I do have an original -- it's a one-page document but I think it's probably easier if the general has an original or a photocopy of the original just so -- the scrolling is sometimes difficult. Okay. This, again, is from Tolimir, from Rogatica, the 1st Podrinje Light Infantry Brigade. This one is dated 21 July, which is of course close to the time that you were at the Jela restaurant, which was the 20th of July. Again marked "very urgent." And this one is personally to General Miletic entitled, "The situation in Zepa." And it's, we can see, providing information about the evacuation of the population, and that the Muslims are shooting at the UNPROFOR base in order to provoke NATO's action. Suggesting that the UNPROFOR and international organisations not be allowed to come into the area. And number 4 he says, "We believe that we would be in a more advantageous position for direct negotiations after we inflict losses on the enemy's military personnel." That's of course an appropriate strategy in any wartime negotiation, I -- would you agree with me on that, General?

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm sorry, I was busy reading. Could you repeat the question?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Yes. I should have let you read that first. I'm just asking about the paragraph 4 where it says that, "We believe that we would be in a more advantageous position for direct negotiations after we inflict losses on enemy's military personnel," and I've said would you agree with me that that's of course appropriate conduct in a war and that can help negotiations if you're in a stronger military position?

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, first of all, let me say what I think about this document. It's a completely legal document. General Tolimir is suggesting something while not being able to get in touch with the commander of the Main Staff because he simply doesn't know where the commander is. So he's sending this document to General Miletic personally, knowing that Miletic is certainly at the Main Staff, and that he will convey the information to General Mladic, who would make a decision. You're asking me if it is normal in the context of negotiations to threaten with weapons, et cetera. Unfortunately, war is not diplomacy. In war, you negotiate from the positions of power. The UNPROFOR in this context is usually the mediator in negotiations. Muslims are trying to push the UNPROFOR to accept Muslim conditions. So Tolimir is suggesting we do the same so we get into a position of power, namely, threatening that the Muslims have to agree to certain conditions; otherwise, we would attack, as has happened before.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Understood. Now let's go to paragraph 5. And it says, "The most propitious means of their destruction would be uses of chemical weapons or aerosol grenades and bombs. Using these means we would accelerate the surrender of Muslims and the fall of Zepa." And I don't want to overdo this chemical weapons thing. Can you tell us what he is likely talking about when he says chemical weapons? If you know?

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Regardless of what General Tolimir is talking about here, this is not usual and it's not allowed. It is not allowed to use chemical weapons in traditional warfare. When I say traditional warfare, I mean one that does not allow for biological, chemical or nuclear weapons, so Tolimir was not supposed to even suggest this to the commander. And the commander, if he's a mature one, would never accept such a proposal. I personally did not approve of this passage at all.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay. I think most armies in the world had or -- and have collections of chemical weapons in their arsenals and I believe the JNA did. Can you tell us what the options of chemical weapons would be in this so we can get an idea of maybe what he would be referring to?

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You mean the technical means allowing for chemical weapons to be used? Do you mean the technology used in order to apply chemical weapons?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: No, I don't mean the delivery means such as mortars or artillery or aerial bombs or anything like that. I'm asking about the chemical itself. What if -- in fact did you know did the JNA have chemicals? I mean all these armies, as you know, had chemical weapons. Some are worse than others, and I just want to get your view, if you can, what in the context of the Zepa environment those -- what might be used in that context.

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I learned at school, there are five types of chemical weapons: One --

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Excuse me, General. I think the Judges were deliberating, and they need to hear you, I'm sorry, if we could give --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Go ahead, General, if you can answer that question. You said, "As far as I learned in school, there are five types of chemical weapons." What we are interested in is what kind of chemical weapons the JNA had, just that, please. Yes, Madam Fauveau?

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, I do not see the pertinence, the relevance of this question, which kind of chemical weapons did the JNA have four years after it ceased to exist. If the Prosecutor wants to ask what kind of chemical weapons were in the possession of the VRS, that's a different thing, but I don't see why he's asking about the JNA.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: The question, if he puts that question, the answer is going to be yes, and it takes us back to square one. So let's -- I don't think you need to comment. Let's proceed, because the witness has already said that they inherited lock, stock and barrel what the JNA had before and what was in their possession. Yes, go ahead, General, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I think, to cut a long story short, all armies in the world have chemical weapons and all of them know they are not allowed to use it, and the justification we all use when we are to answer why we have it in the first place is to respond to the enemy's chemical attack. Now, this was one day after I was attacked by the enemy, by Croats, at Italian's peak and I lost 56 of my soldiers when attacked by chemical weapons by the Croats, but this is no justification. I'm saying again Tolimir should not have called for use of chemical weapons.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Can you just quickly --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: How much more time do you need?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Maybe five minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. And do you still think that -- you won't be able to finish by 10.30, then. Mr. Nicholls and Mr. Ostojic, do you still need 30 minutes and 30 minutes?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: For the next --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: For the next witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: I think I need about half an hour or less, Your Honour. That's my estimate.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: And you, Mr. Ostojic?

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Anywhere from 45 to an hour, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. Okay. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And could you just list us the potential options for chemical weapons that -- I think you said there were five types.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Madam Fauveau?

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we agree that these were the weapons that the VRS had in July 1995 or are we going to seek from the general to -- an explanation what kind of -- what five kinds of chemical weapons any army could have had?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: We are only interested in what the VRS had at the time, I mean, obviously.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Mr. President, I'd like to stick with the JNA if we could and then perhaps then move, like you said.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: The JNA was May -- May 1992. The General yesterday explained the transitory period between the official creation of the VRS on the 12th of May of 1992 and its effective coming into existence on the 23rd, I think, of May of 1992. After that, to my knowledge, chemical weapons also have a shelf life. So -- and perhaps that can be confirmed by the witness. So what we are -- what is relevant for the case is the time period, time frame, when Tolimir is writing about these chemical weapons and that obviously refers to what the VRS had at the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President, I understand and I agree and I was getting there. I just wanted to start with that foundational JNA, then VJ, then VRS, but we can just cut to the chase and --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I think so. I mean, yes, in the meantime I notice Mr. Bourgon.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. President. I simply note for the record that the issue of chemical weapons was not raised in direct examination, it was not discussed in cross-examination, and now we are going completely beyond the scope of what this witness is to bring to this trial, to contribute to this trial. It's not an issue in the indictment. No one is accused of using chemical weapons. My colleague has announced at the beginning of this morning, he said, I've got about 20 minutes and --

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: I'm going to object if we are going to go into a long rambling speech to be --

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Well, we are.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: -- outside the presence of the witness --

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: We are, we are.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Please, please, please, Mr. Bourgon, Mr. Bourgon.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: He keeps interrupting, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: It's not me.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: He shouldn't have said "rambling," attributed "rambling" to your speech for -- to start but you shouldn't have reacted the way you did. The way I'm used to and my colleagues are used to is, if you feel aggrieved, you seek the protection of the Trial Chamber and we do it in a civilised way, in a calm way, without pointing fingers and without raising our voices. Agreed?

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Fully agree, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. So Mr. McCloskey, can you please comment on the substantive part of his intervention?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: The principal reason I'm using this document was because it's personally directed to General Miletic so that I can ask the general how this fits into his position at the time that he has described pursuant to Defence questions and the substantive matter of the document is relevant to that, and if I can get through the document, I think you'll see what I'm getting at and I think the Court will understand the document better, they'll understand General Miletic's role better in the receipt of these kinds of documents and the kind of information that he would be getting but I -- besides that, I don't want to go into it. I can go into it, but we should do it outside the presence of the witness so we don't waste his time and distract him and --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Madam Fauveau?

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, for three days the witness has been explaining the role of General Miletic. I think we all understood that Miletic received documents from the front line and transmitted them to the commander. I don't see what influence the contents of any document can have on the role of General Miletic that simply transmitted that information to the commander or anybody else.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Don't you think it would benefit you if there is an explanation rather than have a document which on the face of it presents you with what it does? It's up to you, but let me confer with my colleagues, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Could I respond just briefly?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Ms. Fauveau states her defence that General Miletic is a transmitter of documents. This is the whole point that I'm getting into this document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: This is precisely why I have made the comment that I did -- that I made.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Madam Fauveau?

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, without going into an argument, I do have to oppose the way the Prosecutor presented these documents. This document has absolutely no influence on the role of General Miletic as a person who was transmitting documents. If somebody wants to say that General Miletic is responsible for something that somebody else wrote in a document --

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: I'm sorry, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: We can't have this in the witness's presence. Our position -- please, Madam Fauveau. Our position is as follows: We don't believe we ought to go for any intent and purposes into the details regarding the existence, nature of chemical weapons in possession of the VRS at the time. It is relevant only insofar as chemical weapons are mentioned in this document allegedly signed by General Tolimir and addressed to General Miletic. I think, having heard you, as well, Mr. McCloskey, you should restrict yourself to asking the witness why would General Tolimir speak or address out of all people General Miletic in relation regarding the possible use of chemical weapons and we move ahead.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: I understand and I think that's a very good question. The point that I'm trying to make with chemical weapons is there a particular chemical weapon that is tear gas and it's not a very heavy chemical weapon and that may be what we are talking about here and I don't want to leave the impression that this is mustard gas. That's what I'm trying to get to. We don't know what it is but tear gas was in the possession of -- I believe, and that's what I want to bring up so we don't believe the impression that this might be some killer --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: You're testifying.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Can I make my speech, too?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: I tried --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Bourgon. I don't think there is need for it. But I suppose -- I suggest that you proceed with the question that we have indicated and we proceed from there.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: And again, please keep calm. I mean it's very important. I know everyone is tired. The witness is tired too. So let's --

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And I will.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: The question is: Why would General Tolimir speak or address of all people to General Miletic in relation to the possible use of chemical weapons?

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I have answered that question at the beginning of debate on this document. Because General Miletic was the only general who was in his place at the Main Staff, and he was able to convey this opinion of General Tolimir to General Mladic. No more than that. Miletic was not asked to answer, just to be a go-between because Tolimir didn't know who his commander was -- where his commander was. Sorry.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay. The last paragraph says, "We believe" --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Can I --

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: -- clarify? If General Miletic was the only person in the Main Staff, why did he have to put personally to General Miletic? If he's the only person, then he would see the document naturally.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] General Tolimir was the assistant commander for intelligence and security. In order to avoid any confusion, it is possible, when the typist received this document from Tolimir, that he gave it to one of his organs who were at the command post at the time. If he was not entitled to have contacts with the commander, he could have been a lower ranking officer. He could have received the document, he could have given it to somebody who would then in turn still have to come to Miletic to ask him what to do with the document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right. The last part, "We believe that we could force Muslims to surrender sooner if we would destroy groups of Muslim refugees fleeing in the direction of Stublic, Radava and Brloska Planina." Now, that particular information personally to General Miletic, first of all --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. One moment because I notice Madam Fauveau.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I really don't understand why we are going into the details of this document that was signed by a third person who at least for the time being is not part of this case. General Miletic cannot be held responsible for something that another person drafted, and the Prosecutor has not provided any evidence that some actions were taken on the basis of this particular document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Let's hear the question first because the question as such hasn't been asked as yet. Yes, Mr. McCloskey, could you get to what your question is? Go ahead.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Is this an appropriate or a legal military -- or not legal but what is his view of this statement about destroying Muslim refugees?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: His, it means Tolimir's?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't know what General Tolimir meant when he wrote this.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Is it allowable in your army to destroy groups of refugees that are leaving?

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. That's a different issue, but it is not allowable.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: If army is mixed into those refugees, is that another issue, which I won't get into but just to clarify it? If there are army mixed in with the refugees, can that be a legitimate target, in your army?

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It cannot be considered a legitimate army, if the army is not opening fire. I've told you already that the Muslims often used civilians as human shield for their own army.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right. Then my question would be the same as the previous paragraph. Why, if you know, would Tolimir be choosing to tell General Miletic, in particular, that his -- what appears -- his opinion that "we believe we could force the Muslims could surrender sooner if we could destroy the refugees"? Why would he pick out Miletic in particular for such a statement? If you know. Or if it's the same answer as before, we can --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Madam Fauveau?

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, I believe that the witness has already answered on several occasions that General Miletic conveyed information to General Mladic, that this was his function in the Main Staff, and I really --

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Objection, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] -- don't see why this question is being asked again.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated]

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Please, I see that is a little bit too much electricity around today. Mr. McCloskey, Ms. Fauveau was still addressing the Chamber. You should have waited until she had finished and then I would have given you the floor, after which Mr. Bourgon would have had his. So let's go back and do this in a civilised way, as I said. Madam Fauveau? Could you please conclude your objection?

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, actually, I was at the end of my objection. I was just going to say that the witness has already repeated on several occasions that General Miletic conveyed documents that arrived at the Main Staff to General Mladic, and I don't know why this question is being asked with regard to every single paragraph of this document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Still, Mr. McCloskey, at the end of his intervention, not the one that he made when you were still addressing the Chamber -- before -- was an invitation to the witness that if his answer is the same as before, we don't need to bother, let's move on. So I think we can calm things down and the general, with his sense of discipline, will understand me perfectly well. If your answer is as it was to the previous question, just tell us yes, and we move forward.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. This would have been the same answer for the third time. Miletic was just an intermediary in conveying orders from one person to another.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. Mr. McCloskey, before you proceed with your next question, do you wish to address the Chamber?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: No, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. And Mr. Bourgon, I take it that you also do not need to address the Chamber.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: There is no need, Mr. President, thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Please calm down. Let's finish the week as -- in an acceptable manner. Yes, Mr. McCloskey.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: General, is it possible that the chemical weapon referred to here by General Tolimir to General Miletic is a form of tear gas called CS, which is relatively non-toxic?

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: We did not have any other chemical agents. What we had, we got from the police. Those were tear gases used by the police and the artillery ammunition, every fifth grenade in keeping with the JNA rules, was filled with one of the chemical agents, either a tear gas or the choking agent. Tear gas is not toxic, where the choking agent does leave some consequences.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Thank you very much, General. I have no further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you. Yes, Mr. Zivanovic? Mr. Bourgon? Let's take one by one. I see four already. Yes, Mr. Zivanovic?

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. With your leave I would like to ask just one question relative to his answer on page 24, lines from 14 to 16, and the question was about legitimate targets, if the army is mixed with the refugees. This is what I would like to put a question to the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Let's hear the question and that would make it easier for us to decide. Address it to us, please, first, and General, you don't answer it before we give you the green light.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In the witness's answer, it says that this target cannot be considered legitimate if the army is not opening fire. Further cross-examination by Mr. Zivanovic:

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: My question to the witness is this: Can this be considered a legitimate target if the army mixed with the refugees, irrespective of the fact that it is not opening fire, is advancing and coming on to the territory under the control of the army of Republika Srpska? In other words, can the army go anywhere if it's mixed with the refugees irrespective of the fact that it is not opening fire and whether this action must be tolerated by the VRS?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. Thank you. You've got the green light. Go ahead. If you can answer that question or this question.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Even in this case, fire cannot be opened because the intermediaries in the war exist for that. In this particular case, it is UNPROFOR and UNPROFOR should be addressed and sought protection from.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can I ask a very specific question? If UNPROFOR is not there, we had situations that the 28th Division was withdrawing from Jaglici and Susnjar after the fall of Srebrenica through the territory of the Republika Srpska army towards Kladanj and Tuzla. There was no UNPROFOR there. Does the witness consider that even if this case--

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Slow down.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: [Interpretation] There was no basis for opening fire on these forces?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: One moment, General. Yes, Mr. Josse?

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Objection, Your Honour. This is trying to make this witness into an expert. He's never been put forward as an expert and in our submission, this line of cross-examination should not be allowed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: We are actually delving into legal matters, not exactly military matters. But I need to confer with my colleagues.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: We are deciding in a very simple, straightforward matter, without needing to decide on your objection, Mr. Josse. Our position is that we have heard enough on this and we don't need the general to answer the question, the second question that Mr. Zivanovic put. Any -- I had noticed earlier on Mr. Bourgon, Madam Fauveau and Mr. Krgovic, in that order. Mr. Bourgon, do you wish to put a question?

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. I would like to ask to -- with leave of the Court, I would like to ask a question to the witness concerning something that was raised, a new issue that was raised by my colleague on page 3, line 9.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: On page?

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Page 3, line 9.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: One moment. I have to go back to page 3. Yes. Please address the question to us first and then we decide if to authorise it or not.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. The question is very simple. The -- my colleague has put the question to the witness, two questions, as a matter of fact, which relates with the responsibility for prisoner of war at the brigade level and also the answer, what was the responsibility of the chief of security at the brigade level. Those issues were not part of the direct examination, they were not raised on cross, and that's what I would like to ask a couple of questions to the witness concerning both of these issues.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Go ahead. Go ahead.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. Further cross-examination by Mr. Bourgon:

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Good morning, General. I just have a few additional questions for you. On page 3, at lines number 7 to 9, your answer to my colleague's questions was the following: "When it comes to the use of the military police, the person in charge is the security organ, regardless of the issue, be it the prisoners of war, escorting convoys or any other police task." And my question is simply, would you agree with me, General, that the role of the chief of the security is to advise the commander on the use and the combat readiness of the military police?

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And General, would you agree with me that the chief of security has no command authority over the military police in the brigade?

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He does not have direct command authority, but he orders the commander of the battalion of the military police what to do with the police, but he is not the one to assign military policemen to various groups. In the army, there is the term control and command. He has the controlling role when it comes to the police.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And any orders that the chief of security would, and I say orders or instructions, or -- that would be assigned to the military police would come from his commander; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is a very ambiguous question. I suppose you meant the commander who is the chief of security's superior? Is that what you meant?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Exactly, exactly, General. Simply for you to confirm that although he may have a coordination or controlling role, he does not issue orders that come from him to the military police. He has no authority to do that?

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct. He does not have the authority to command the police. He can propose the commander to use the military police, and if the commander agrees to that then he conveys the commander's orders and he gives instructions to the commander of the military police battalion or company as to what to do, how to proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Thank you very much, General.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Just one moment. Yes, I had noticed you, Madam Fauveau.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, I will probably not have any more questions for this witness. I will not ask for your permission to allow me to put questions to the witness, in other words.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. Doesn't mean that you will put questions without -- okay. Thank you. Mr. Josse?

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: The Chamber will be relieved to hear that our position is the same.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Judge Kwon, do you have any questions to ask? General, we've come to the end of your testimony, which means you're free to go. I wish to thank you on behalf of the Trial Chamber, Judge Kwon, Judge Prost, Judge Stole, who is not with us today, also on behalf of the Tribunal and on behalf of everyone present here we all wish you a safe journey back home. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Bourgon?

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. With your permission, after the break, I would like, Mr. President, to address the Court concerning the scope of re-examination and the way re-examination is being conducted, and I cannot do it at this time because I need to consult my colleagues, but I would like to address the Court because, I think that this situation is getting out of hand. Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Documents? Yes, Mr. McCloskey?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Yeah. I've got a list of 65 ter, 29, that's directive 4.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: It has been circulated. Is it still as it was when it was circulated?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Everything but the 2669 A and B. That, you can just cross off the list.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. Any objections from any of the Defence teams?

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Could we have a moment, please? We've literally just been given this list, and it includes a number of the documents that were used in the re-examination, and I think we would appreciate the break before we make any submissions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. That's fair enough. We'll give you a break. 25 minutes. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. Exhibits. So Mr. Josse?

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Your Honour, on behalf of General Gvero we object to the admission of 65 ter numbers 45 and 131. For the most part the submission is the same in relation to both of them, although needless to say, the Chamber will need to consider each separately before coming to a decision. We contend that because the witness had no firsthand knowledge of these documents, he conceded that he had never seen them before, it is not proper for them to be admitted through him. In effect, the evidence that he gave in relation to these documents was both speculative, in effect opinion evidence, and that amounted, we submit, to evidence that at the very best could be said to be expert evidence and this witness has never been admitted as an expert pursuant to Rule 94. In addition to that, as I've already said, if the Chamber is against us so far as that submission is concerned, the answers the witness gave in relation to the documents are highly speculative and rely on his opinion. Moving on from that, there's a further ground of objection, and that relates to the way these have been dealt with procedurally. I know that my learned friend, Mr. Bourgon, alluded to the fact that he wished to address the Chamber at some point about to the way things are being done in terms of re-examination, and of course, there is proper re-examination and improper re-examination. But we note and we ask the Trial Chamber to take into consideration the fact that neither of these documents were on the original list of documents, index of documents, perhaps I should say, that the Prosecution provided to us in relation to General Milovanovic. There were a large number of documents on that particular list but neither 45 nor 131 were on that list. And then to use them in re-examination is in this way is one thing but then to seek their admission into evidence is another thing. Of course, I accept that they are on the 65 ter list, they have 65 ter numbers, but nonetheless, it's one thing for them to have 65 ter numbers and it's quite another thing for the Prosecution not to put them on their list as potential documents for use during the testimony of the witness. I should add in passing the cross-examination that allowed the Prosecution to use these in re-examination was not surprising cross-examination. If Mr. Krgovic in the course of that cross-examination had asked questions which were completely out of the blue and surprising, then that would be another thing, but they weren't. It was standard cross-examination bearing in mind the issues in the case as far as General Gvero is concerned, and then to seek the admission of these documents through this back door route, we submit is highly objectionable. Your Honour, in any event, we put the Prosecution to proof as to the authenticity of both these documents and, finally, and I have nearly finished, one small matter. So far as 131 is concerned, there is a small translation issue which we will need to address with either the court officer or the Prosecution and so the translation as it stands at the moment is not accepted, but that's a separate issue. But for the reasons I've outlined, we object to the admission of these documents.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you, Mr. Josse. Mr. McCloskey? If you could address the various --

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: But I notice also Madam Bourgon -- Madam Fauveau. Not yet.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: If I could go first because --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, I think -- I would suggest that he deals --

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In fact, I believe it would be easier to do it together because I subscribe to the objection made by my colleague and I take into account document 2554 -- sorry, 2754.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: In other words, you're adding to the objection also 2754 on the same basis, on the same grounds?

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. Thank you. Thank you, Madam Fauveau. Mr. McCloskey? If you could take up the submissions one by one, please?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Yes. The first that I noted was the argument that the witness did not know of the document or was not part of the document, that argument. And of course, Mr. President, we have for many months now had many, many comments from witnesses on documents that they knew nothing whatsoever about but were in a position to offer views on them. I don't need to use examples. You know them. The Zepa exhibits, for example. And the reason that I believe that you allowed the testimony for the various documents is because of the position of this witness, what he had testified to on direct and cross-examination, and that I think he had valuable insight into the people and the processes, which is what this was all about. So I think if we look at our previous practices and the way that your -- you allowed this evidence in, I don't see any problem whatsoever on -- based on that objection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Will you have anyone else dealing more specifically with these two documents, 45, 131, and perhaps also 2754?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Well, that's a good question, because General Smith was down for some of these documents, Rick Butler was down for some of these documents, but frankly, after the evidence from this witness, I'm not sure we need to. We can. It's not difficult. And it can come in through someone else if there is any concern whatsoever. And that's -- so that's not a problem. I think as we review what this witness has said about these documents, we hope to restrict some of our evidence that we had in line. Now regarding the objection related to speculativeness, I don't think there was anything speculative about what he was saying. Had it been speculative, I would have trusted the Court to have not allowed any further questions or answers on it, as the Court has done throughout. I thought his insights, while I didn't always agree with him, were valuable and something the Court should see and I don't think that's any grounds whatsoever. And if it had been, the Court would have dealt with it. Not on the original list; well, we have the 65 ter list.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I don't think you need to address that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: We know what the practice has been when it comes to redirect. There is also authenticity, the authenticity issue.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Yes. Of course, it's our burden to provide authenticity. These documents are coming from the same collections from the documents that have been used massively by the Defence. However, on particular cases, where there is concern, we will provide the -- more evidence of that. In fact, I can tell you that the -- just from my memory, the 13 July document about prisoners and separating prisoners from other prisoners, that document is an original document that was brought to us by Major Obrenovic when he plead guilty. And so that will of course need his testimony to authenticate and you'll here the history of that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Which also means that you can use that document direct with Major Obrenovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Absolutely.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yeah.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Absolutely. And the fewer I can use with Major Obrenovic, the better, but if there is an authenticity issue, of course.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. I think I can stop you there, Mr. McCloskey, provided my colleagues agree with me. I think we can do exactly as we did with the previous witness. We can mark these for identification pending the authentication issue. And also the possibility that there may be used more directly and more specifically with some other witness. We leave them marked for identification in the meantime, but I need to confer.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And Mr. President, so I won't -- Ms. Stewart tells me that on your list there is 65 ter 849, which is something I didn't use, so don't -- so cross that one off your list as well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Our decision is that we will mark these three documents, that is 65 ter number 45, 65 ter number 131, and 65 ter number 2754, for identification purposes only, pending proof of their authenticity. This is the only ground that we are accepting for the basis of not admitting them now and marking them for identification purposes only. The rest are admitted provided they are all translated, which I think they are. We come to the Miletic exhibits. Madam Fauveau, you have got seven documents that you wish to tender. With the exception of the last one, I take it that none have been translated to date? Correct me if I'm wrong.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, there are two that have been translated, in fact, one which was originally in English, 5D391; one has been translated, P150; and the others were marked for identification pending translation. [In English] 5D390.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: 390. I was going to ask to you correct that, in fact. So P150 has been translated already. 390 has been translated already. The rest will remain marked for identification in any case, pending translation, but there is any objection on your part, Mr. McCloskey?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: These come from these same collections but no, I will not object.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. Thank you. Any objection from any of the other Defence teams? None. So P150 and P390 are admitted. The remainder will remain marked for identification pending translation, official translation thereof. Yes, Madam Fauveau.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, I still have to respond to the Prosecution. I don't know from which collection these documents originate, but in any case, they all bear the signature of the witness we have just heard.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: I'm speaking about a typewritten signature, not a handwritten one.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I don't think we need to delve into this. So exhibits tendered -- to be tendered by the Gvero team? There is only one to my knowledge and that's 6D129.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: And I take it this has been translated.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: It has now, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. Any objection, Mr. McCloskey?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: No, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Any of the other Defence teams wishes to object to the admission of this document? None. So this will become an exhibit. Thank you. Mr. Sarapa, yes?

utterances.speaker: MR. SARAPA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Just one document for identification since the translation is pending, 7D460.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Any objection, Mr. McCloskey?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: No, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Other Defence teams, any objection? None. It will be marked for identification pending translation thereof. Thank you. Next witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And if possible, Mr. President, if I could have maybe five minutes at the end to speak of a matter in private session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Good morning to you, Mr. Simic.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: And welcome to this Tribunal. You're about to start giving evidence. Before you do so, our rules require that you make a solemn declaration, just equivalent to an oath in some jurisdictions, to the effect that in the course of your testimony, you undertake to speak the truth, the whole truth and nothing but the truth. The text is going to be handed to you now. Please read it out aloud and that will be your solemn undertaking with us.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you, sir. Please make yourself comfortable.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. Nicholls will put some questions to you. He will then be followed on cross-examination by one or more of the Defence teams. Mr. Nicholls?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Good morning, sir.

utterances.speaker: SREDOJE SIMIC
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: I have not too many questions for you today and I'll try to get through it as quickly as we can. Could you please tell us your full name?

utterances.speaker: SREDOJE SIMIC
utterances.text: My name is Sredoje Simic.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: When were you born, sir?

utterances.speaker: SREDOJE SIMIC
utterances.text: I was born on the 2nd January 1952 in Vrsac. It's a place in Vojvodina, Republic of Serbia.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Thank you. And could you tell me what your employment is at present? Where do you work?

utterances.speaker: SREDOJE SIMIC
utterances.text: I currently work in a weekly called Svedok, which means witness in Belgrade.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: And you're a journalist with that magazine, correct?

utterances.speaker: SREDOJE SIMIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Could you very briefly tell me about your educational background, in just a few sentences, if you can?

utterances.speaker: SREDOJE SIMIC
utterances.text: Well, I went to primary school in Pirana, Rijeka in Slovenia and in Karlovac in Croatia, and I finished university in Zagreb.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: And you received a degree in law, if I'm correct; is that right?

utterances.speaker: SREDOJE SIMIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: When did you begin your career as a journalist?

utterances.speaker: SREDOJE SIMIC
utterances.text: I began in March or April 1975, as a journalist.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: And except for relatively brief periods, is it safe to say you've been a journalist since that time, for over 30 years?

utterances.speaker: SREDOJE SIMIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: I want to now ask you some questions about an article you wrote and could we please have 00480 in e-court? If we could go to page 2? Got a problem.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: I do have a hard copy if this looks like a long problem. Oh, there we go.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Now, sir, I think you'll recognise this but do you recognise this article?

utterances.speaker: SREDOJE SIMIC
utterances.text: I don't see the document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. One moment.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I see it now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Is it okay now? It's okay now but -- because we had the document but we were informed that the witness didn't.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, could you just tell us, what is the title or headline of this article?

utterances.speaker: SREDOJE SIMIC
utterances.text: "I am not ashamed of any of my" -- and I can't see the rest.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: You're having difficulty reading the -- oh, I see. It's because it's on two pages. If I could give the witness a hard copy, unless we can bring up both pages together?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I think if we bring the two pages together, it will so minuscule no one will be able to see it.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] "I am not ashamed of anything I did, and if I need to be put on trial, let that be in my country."

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Okay. What is the date of this article?

utterances.speaker: SREDOJE SIMIC
utterances.text: 20th October 2002.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: And who wrote this article?

utterances.speaker: SREDOJE SIMIC
utterances.text: I am the author of the interview.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: And the person interviewed in this article, who did you interview for this article?

utterances.speaker: SREDOJE SIMIC
utterances.text: I did an interview with Colonel Ljubisa Beara, Colonel of the army of Republika Srpska.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Okay. Now, the article was published on 29 October. Can you tell us when the interview took place? How soon was it before the publication of the article?

utterances.speaker: SREDOJE SIMIC
utterances.text: The interview took place over the course of two or three days, but it was five years ago, and the interview took place after the moment when it became known that the indictment against Ljubisa Beara was opened.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Thank you. Your Honours, I think my friend was indicating to me that he heard a mistake in the translation. I'm not sure if that's what I understood from my friend.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Ostojic?

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. I would just ask the Court to inquire on page 42, line 24, I think there is no dispute as to the length of the interview and that it, in our view, is not accurate how it was translated, so if we could maybe restate it or have him tell us again, when the interview happened, how long the interview took and then how soon before the publication of the interview did the interview actually take place, which is where I think we may have a little misunderstanding.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: And the fact that it would reflect the essence, the gist of your question in the first place.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Was this two or three days or two or three hours, the duration of the interview?

utterances.speaker: SREDOJE SIMIC
utterances.text: The interview took two hours or just a bit over two hours. But it was two or three days after information agencies published that the indictment against Ljubisa Beara was made public.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, can you tell me, without necessarily giving the names or places of people who helped you, the circumstances of how this interview took place? How were you able to set up an interview with Mr. Beara?

utterances.speaker: SREDOJE SIMIC
utterances.text: I had not known Ljubisa Beara before the interview, although I had heard of him, and I knew that Mr. Vojislav Seslj was attacking him because of an incident that I believe happened sometime in the 1990s between members of the JNA and members of the Serb Radical Party. A couple of months before the indictment against Beara was made public, rumours circulated in Belgrade, especially among journalists, that there would be more indictments raised related to the Srebrenica case, and various names were mentioned, among them the name of Ljubisa Beara. Perhaps a couple of months after the indictment was made public, it crossed my mind that I could make an interview with Mr. Ljubisa Beara because he was interesting, in view of the role, the position, he held at the time of the Srebrenica operation, and on the other hand, very few ICTY indictees were prepared to give interviews. If I remember correctly, we had only managed to get an interview with Mr. Nebojsa Pavkovic and Mr. Perisic. Since I was in charge of army security on the publishing board, I knew a lot of officers, retired and active duty, and I thought that perhaps they might help me get in touch with Mr. Beara, whom I didn't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: And during -- THE TRANSLATOR: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Thank you. And I take it then that you were successful through these contacts in getting in touch with Mr. Beara and setting up this interview?

utterances.speaker: SREDOJE SIMIC
utterances.text: Before the indictment was made public, I was not very active, very persistent in my efforts to find Beara. I was busy doing other things, covering the investigation concerning the murder of Zeljko Raznjatovic, Arkan, but when the indictment was made public I concentrated on this a bit more. I found a contact who promised he would try to get me in touch with Mr. Beara but he wasn't sure that Mr. Beara would accept.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: All right. Now, during the interview, did you use a tape recording device or did you take notes or how did you make a record of what was being satisfied during the interview with Mr. Beara?

utterances.speaker: SREDOJE SIMIC
utterances.text: The interview was tape recorded from its beginning to its end.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: And by "from its beginning to its end," do you mean the entire interview was tape recorded, all of it, on tape?

utterances.speaker: SREDOJE SIMIC
utterances.text: Yes, the complete interview was recorded but not all of it was published. The interview that you've shown to me does not reflect the entire interview I had with Mr. Beara.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: I know you can't be exactly precise but how much of what we have in the article -- how much of the interview with Mr. Beara is contained in the article, in other words, how much of what Mr. Beara told to you doesn't appear anywhere in the article?

utterances.speaker: SREDOJE SIMIC
utterances.text: Well, between 45 and 55 per cent. I can't be more precise than that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Mr. Nicholls, I take it, but you can of course inquire with the witness, that the witness did not keep or preserve the tape.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: I was going to get to that Your Honour, but I can ask him now.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: You can answer this question very simply, you don't need to spend to much time on it, sir, but do you still have the tape of this interview?

utterances.speaker: SREDOJE SIMIC
utterances.text: No. I've already said it twice. The tapes are kept for about half a year in the editorial room. It was very hard at the time to obtain those tapes in Belgrade. They were of poor quality and we reused the tape in order to save the resources.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
