utterances.text: Okay. Now, the portion of what Mr. Beara spoke to you about that's not included in the interview, that you decided to leave out, what was that all about? What did you decide to leave out, if you can tell us generally the topics?

utterances.speaker: SREDOJE SIMIC
utterances.text: I've already said that Mr. Beara was named by Mr. Seslj with regard to that incident in Montenegro and he spoke at great length about that incident. It seemed that it bothered him quite a lot, because he thought that he was not at all to blame for what Mr. Seslj was accusing him. And you could tell by his reactions that he was not very happy with that. I was interested, i.e., my editor was interested in the indictment. He was indicted not for the crime in Montenegro but for Srebrenica and I focused on Srebrenica, and in addition to that, he spoke at great length about himself, about his life, about his family. He was finding all that very hard, I would say.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Now, during the interview did Mr. Beara say anything about Srebrenica that was not included in the article?

utterances.speaker: SREDOJE SIMIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Now, we don't need to bring it up again but we can see, if we look at the article, it's still up, if we scroll down a bit, we can see that part of the format of this article is questions by you put to Mr. Beara and his answers. Now, how accurate is the article as a record of the answers given by Mr. Beara during the interview? In other words, the words we see here spoken by Mr. Beara, are those the same words he actually spoke to you and that were recorded on the tape recording?

utterances.speaker: SREDOJE SIMIC
utterances.text: Yes. When the interview was being prepared for printing, I tried to keep it as authentic as possible. The only thing that were removed from some filler words or some repetitions, where -- places where Mr. Beara repeated himself. But I would say that in essence the interview is original.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: And what about your questions? Did you edit any of the questions that we see printed in the article or were those exactly the same as the way you put the questions to Mr. Beara?

utterances.speaker: SREDOJE SIMIC
utterances.text: Yes, as a matter of fact, but let me explain. When you do an interview you usually put questions rather broadly in order to explain to the interlocutor what you're interested in but when you word your questions for the newspaper, you have to make them as concise and precise as possible. They don't -- they mustn't be leading. And in that part, I would say that the printed questions do not reflect 100 per cent the questions that I actually put to Mr. Beara. The words are different.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: And is that if I understood you, to make them shorter and clearer or perhaps just shorter, your questions?

utterances.speaker: SREDOJE SIMIC
utterances.text: Yes, you understood me well.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: A moment ago you said that in Mr. Beara's answers, you would remove -- the only things you removed were filler words or repetition. What do you mean exactly by filler words?

utterances.speaker: SREDOJE SIMIC
utterances.text: For example, well, actually, as far as I can remember, he used some expressions that are part of the slang. There were some repetitions. Sometimes he would go over the same grounds again. He would repeat the answers that he had given to the previous question.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Okay. And in any of these edits for filler words or repetition, to your mind, in any way, did you change the meaning of his answers at all?

utterances.speaker: SREDOJE SIMIC
utterances.text: No. If you omit a filler word, you don't change the meaning of that sentence, so my answer would be no.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Did Mr. Beara ask to review the text prior to publication? In other words, did he want to see what you were going to actually write before you published it?

utterances.speaker: SREDOJE SIMIC
utterances.text: I believe that I should add something to my previous answer. When Mr. Beara accepted to give me that interview there were three conditions. The first condition was for me to come alone. My contact told me that I should come alone without a photographer or anybody else. The second condition was that no photos should be taken. And the third condition was that I should promise him that I would never tell anybody where the interview had taken place. And we accepted those conditions. When the interview was over, because of the sensitivity of the issues, I offered Mr. Beara to review the interview and without a second thought, he said that that was not necessary and that he had full confidence in me and that he fully believed that I would convey the interview with him accurately.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: After publication of the interview in Svedok, did you receive any feedback, directly or indirectly, from Mr. Beara, about the article?

utterances.speaker: SREDOJE SIMIC
utterances.text: After the interview, I never heard from or saw Mr. Beara, but I did get feedback after a certain time, maybe three, five or even 10 days after the interview, I bumped into the gentleman who put me through to Mr. Beara and he told me that Mr. Beara was extremely satisfied with the interview and that he had no objections whatsoever to the contents thereof.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Thank you. I have no further questions at this point.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you, Mr. Nicholls. Mr. Ostojic or Mr. Meek? I don't know who is -- I think this mainly concerns you. I even doubt if any of the other Defence teams wishes to cross-examine this witness. Yes, go ahead, Mr. Meek.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Simic. How are you?

utterances.speaker: SREDOJE SIMIC
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: You've had a chance to review this article obviously before you came here to testify, correct?

utterances.speaker: SREDOJE SIMIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: You have just testified, by the way, that subsequent to the interview, Mr. Beara never spoke to you personally, nor did you ever see him again; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: SREDOJE SIMIC
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: If we could, could we have put on the e-court document 2D127? It's an OTP information report, for the record, dated 16 December 2005.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Nicholls?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: I have no objection, but apparently we have not yet received -- we don't have the list of cross exhibits. If that's available I'd like a copy but I don't object to him continuing.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: Your Honour, I would apologise for that. Our case manager's -- yesterday her grandfather is in the hospital and I think he passed away and she suddenly left the office, and I apologise, my friend. There's only 480, which you already have in, the OTP information report, 2D127.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yeah. Go ahead.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: I'm sorry. The statement provided to the Belgrade district court of 24 March 2006, it would be 2D128. And the OTP supplemental information sheet dated 30 May 2007, it would be 2D129.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Meek?

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: Mr. Simic, there were a few mistakes in that article, were there not, in life we make a few mistakes?

utterances.speaker: SREDOJE SIMIC
utterances.text: What mistakes are you referring to?

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: Well, first off, if you could look at the 65 ter 480, I don't know what page it would be in B/C/S but page 4 in English -- no.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: Now I'm at the article, Your Honour. Keep that on there for a second. Okay. We will go to the actual article.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Do you have an idea of which part of the article in the original it is? Because --

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: Approximately page 2, under the heading -- page 2 or -- under the heading in bold the picture that says, "If they think I must go to The Hague, let them find me and arrest me." And I think the witness actually has the article in front of him in hard copy.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: But the article is a long article. He needs to be --

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: Let me read this to you. Just let me read this to you real briefly. You state in your article that as soon as the unsealed indictment against him appeared on the official site of The Hague Tribunal, the courageous Sarajevan Beara left his Belgrade flat and went into hiding. Do you remember him telling you that?

utterances.speaker: SREDOJE SIMIC
utterances.text: I'm afraid I don't understand your question. What do you want me to say?

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: I'm going to find it for you in the B/C/S/Serbian, sir, so you can look at it. At the beginning of the article, Mr. Simic, your picture, if you could -- Mr. Simic, just put the article over one page that you have in front of you. Below your picture.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Let's be more practical. What I suggest, Madam Usher, you approach Mr. Meek and his assistant. They will show you exactly which part of the article they are referring to and then you show it to the witness and we proceed like that.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: If it helps if my friend wants, I've got a larger copy that's much easier to read in hard copy.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. You can use that.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: He can have it if you like.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, I've been able to locate that part.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: That's good. And I thank you for that, Mr. Simic.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I've lost it again. Now it's good.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, your question now, Mr. Meek?

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: Mr. Simic, you see the short paragraph that says, "As soon as the indictment, sealed indictment against him appeared on the official site," do you see that, sir? And you write that Mr. Beara had left his Belgrade flat, correct?

utterances.speaker: SREDOJE SIMIC
utterances.text: Yes. I can see that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: Now, on the very front of the article, where it starts, you have a -- we may have to go back to the very first page. Okay. It's a byline I think that you wrote, Mr. Simic, under one of the pictures, that says, "senior officer of the army of Republika Srpska" -- there you go, top right up there -- "senior officer of the army of Republika Srpska Ljubisa Beara who ended up on the list." You see that, sir?

utterances.speaker: SREDOJE SIMIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: Now, in that, that's just your -- that's your writing, correct?

utterances.speaker: SREDOJE SIMIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: Now, if you'll notice there, you say that he left his comfortable flat and went into hiding, when in fact, when you tape recorded his interview, it was just a flat, correct?

utterances.speaker: SREDOJE SIMIC
utterances.text: The comfortable flat is just a matter of style. To me, every flat that somebody owns or somebody lives is comfortable. Hiding might be somewhat far-fetched. I heard from a gentleman whom I had contacted in order to get to Mr. Beara that he was no longer in his apartment and that he went somewhere else to find shelter. I never visited Mr. Beara in his apartment. We conducted this interview at a different place.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: Thank you. So not only did you never enter any apartment or flat of Mr. Beara's, he never referred to his flat or apartment as being comfortable or plush or anything like that? You agree with that, sir?

utterances.speaker: SREDOJE SIMIC
utterances.text: Yes. That was my opinion, my poetic licence, if you will. This is what you do when you edit your own text.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: Now, could we show on the screen briefly the 2D127? It would be the OTP information report. Paragraph 4, I believe. Now, do you recall first, Mr. Simic, meeting with an OTP investigator named Bursik on or about 16 December 2005?

utterances.speaker: SREDOJE SIMIC
utterances.text: Yes. My secretary called me when they came. I was just being discharged from the hospital. I was ill at the time. So I was leaving the hospital. I took a taxi and went there.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: And sir, how long did the -- was it an interview type situation, where the investigator asked you questions and you answered them?

utterances.speaker: SREDOJE SIMIC
utterances.text: Well, in my view, it was just an exchange of information. Obviously they did ask me questions. He asked me about the interview, how this came about. He was interested in the tape. He asked me if I could possibly find the tape. I promised I would. And if I did find it, that I would hand it over to The Hague Tribunal, i.e., to the OTP.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: Thank you. Two follow-up questions. Do you recall whether the investigator had a tape recorder and tape recorded that meeting?

utterances.speaker: SREDOJE SIMIC
utterances.text: There were two investigators actually, and there was a lady interpreter. As far as I can remember, one of the investigators asked me questions and the other made notes of the young lady's words, i.e., of what I had said, and then she interpreted for him.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: Mr. Simic, looking at this information report, which was generated from your meeting with the OTP representatives, including investigator Bursik, do you have any idea why under paragraph 4, they would state that you told them that Ljubisa Beara had telephoned you after the article? Do you have any idea why they would put that in a report when in fact that wasn't the truth and you never told them that?

utterances.speaker: SREDOJE SIMIC
utterances.text: I can see it on the screen myself. This must be a translation error, or maybe the investigator misunderstood the interpreter's words. I said on that occasion, and I repeated it before the special court in Belgrade, that after the interview several readers called the newspaper to commend the interview and they also had comments about Mr. Beara as an army officer. I never stated that Mr. Beara had called me. He did not even have my number. So there was no way for him to call me. This must be a mistake. I did say during the interview that several people called the newspaper after the interview, and this must have been misinterpreted or misunderstood as Beara calling me. I've already said that the person who put me through to him told me that Mr. Beara was pleased with the article.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone for Mr. Meek.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: Thank you, sir. Mr. Simic, during this article, Ljubisa Beara told you, in fact, that he did not participate in the preparing of the operation of the Serbian forces entering Srebrenica, correct?

utterances.speaker: SREDOJE SIMIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: He also told you that he did not know what was being prepared regarding Srebrenica, correct?

utterances.speaker: SREDOJE SIMIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: He also told you that when the Srebrenica operation started, that he personally was on the Bihac front. He told you that too, didn't he?

utterances.speaker: SREDOJE SIMIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: Then at one point in your article, after he tells you that he was on the Bihac front and had returned, by the time he returned the Srebrenica action was completely over, correct?

utterances.speaker: SREDOJE SIMIC
utterances.text: This is what transpires from his words.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: Now, right after that, at least in the English translation, you have Mr. Beara saying, "One day, when I was taking the mail to General Mladic I saw a large number of buses on all the roads leading from Bratunac to Zepa to Srebrenica." Do you recall that?

utterances.speaker: SREDOJE SIMIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: Now, sir, I'm not a native speaker of Serbian and I don't obviously know the language, but my friends who are tell me that the saying, "One day, when I was doing something," does not necessarily connote a specific day. Is that true?

utterances.speaker: SREDOJE SIMIC
utterances.text: In principle, according to the rules of grammar, that should be the case, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: And you, sir, as a native Serbian speaker, when it is said like this in an interview, what does that mean to you?

utterances.speaker: SREDOJE SIMIC
utterances.text: That there was a lapse of time. It wasn't yesterday, because he would have said yesterday. It wasn't the day before yesterday. There is a word for the day before yesterday. The way I understood it was that it was some time ago.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: And, sir, when he says, and tells you that he had been on the Bihac front when the Srebrenica action started and did not return until it was over, then he goes on to tell you one day, not previously, but one day I was taking the mail, what -- in the Serbian language, what does that mean to you, sir? Does it mean one day, 10 days, seven days, 14 days?

utterances.speaker: SREDOJE SIMIC
utterances.text: I can't give you a precise answer. I know where Bihac is. I know where Srebrenica is, where the operation took place. And it's very difficult to imagine that in such circumstances it would not take more than one day from Bihac to Srebrenica. It must have been a few days. I wasn't there and I didn't ask him about that. He is probably better suited to say this. But it is obvious that a certain period of time did elapse and that this period was not just one or two days.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: And again, Mr. Simic, just to be clear, that time that had elapsed would have been the time after Srebrenica action was completed and finished, correct?

utterances.speaker: SREDOJE SIMIC
utterances.text: That's the way it seems.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: Mr. Simic, during the interview with Mr. Beara, he also told you, did he not, and when you asked him about mass graves and crimes, he told you, "It is not possible to call out killing in such -- to carry out killing on such a mass scale in the presence of United Nations peacekeepers, even if someone had such an insane idea." Those were his words, correct?

utterances.speaker: SREDOJE SIMIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: Mr. Simic, during the interview, it's true, is it not, that Ljubisa Beara never used any derogatory terms towards Muslims or Croats, correct?

utterances.speaker: SREDOJE SIMIC
utterances.text: No, no, I'm sorry, never.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: Then you talked to Mr. Beara about the Krstic case, did you not?

utterances.speaker: SREDOJE SIMIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: And do you recall that Mr. Beara told you then that he had watched the relay of the trial when the Prosecution had asked Krstic something to the effect of, "So, General, you were not involved in the Srebrenica crime?" Krstic said, "I wasn't." Apparently, thereafter, the-- they showed an intercept or a secret recording between the Chief of Staff of the Zvornik Brigade, Dragan Obrenovic, wherein Krstic allegedly told Obrenovic to kill all the prisoners, the 300 or 400 Muslim prisoners that Obrenovic had reported he was holding. Do you recall that?

utterances.speaker: SREDOJE SIMIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: He further told you, Mr. Beara told you in regards to the Krstic case and the allegations that had been made, that he was shocked, didn't he?

utterances.speaker: SREDOJE SIMIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: And that the papers were writing things about him saying he was a big criminal, correct?

utterances.speaker: SREDOJE SIMIC
utterances.text: Yes. He was very upset, troubled. I said that at the very start, in my testimony. He was very upset and he was taking very hard all those accusations made against him, both the Seslj accusations and the -- those related to Srebrenica.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: And he told you also that these allegations about him being the big war criminal and a big criminal at that time were notorious lies and nonsense, didn't he?

utterances.speaker: SREDOJE SIMIC
utterances.text: I don't recall the exact words he used, but that's what he said, and that's in the interview.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: SREDOJE SIMIC
utterances.text: The interview reflects what he said.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: All right. Now, the -- I'm going to read, help you jog your memory so we can get through this quicker. He told you, and if it was typed out correctly from the interview, that "someone from the Drina Corps allegedly notified me that there were '2.000 parcels'" and asked what to do with them, and I said, "Arrange them in three, four rows." He went on to tell you, "They wanted to say that I ordered the killing of the prisoners." And that's when he said, "This is a notorious lie and nonsense." Do you recall that, sir?

utterances.speaker: SREDOJE SIMIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes. Mr. Beara said that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: Just for the record, several places in the article, you have put quotation marks before and after a word or a group of words, such as you did here before 2000 and after parcels. Do you recall that?

utterances.speaker: SREDOJE SIMIC
utterances.text: Yes. Well, in the Serbian language, how shall I put it, when you want to convey that something is not true, when you want to even mock an allegation, that's an expression you often use.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: You stated that approximately 55 per cent of the taped conversation that took place that day was not used in the article, am I correct, sir?

utterances.speaker: SREDOJE SIMIC
utterances.text: Between 45 and 55 per cent of the material was used. I can't say exactly. It's been five years. But the part that was left out certainly has nothing to do with Srebrenica.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: But a lot of -- a lot -- correct me if I'm wrong, sir, Mr. Simic, a lot of what was left out was Mr. Beara talking to you about the Radical Party leader, Vojislav Seslj, correct?

utterances.speaker: SREDOJE SIMIC
utterances.text: No. You didn't understand me. He wasn't talking about Vojislav Seslj. He was talking about the accusations Seslj was making against him. He was saying that he was being framed, that somebody was trying to accuse him of something he wasn't to be blamed for. I think it involved a vehicle that members of the Serbian Radical Party had stolen from some barracks. He wasn't talking about Seslj defensively. He was kind of saying to me that he had nothing to do with it whatsoever.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: And, Mr. Simic, further, he talked to you about the fact -- and I believe it's even in the article itself and you printed that -- that Seslj was spreading lies about Mr. Beara having killed a thousand Muslims and things like that, correct?

utterances.speaker: SREDOJE SIMIC
utterances.text: I don't recall whether it's in that article. If it's in the article, then Mr. Beara said it.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: Mr. Simic, I'll just point you out and again I don't speak B/C/S, you have the article in front of you, in bold, probably under a picture, you have Mr. Beara quoted as saying, "I lived peacefully until Vojislav Seslj started attacking and slandering me in public. He claimed that I personally killed a thousand Muslim civilians, that I organised the kidnapping of people from a -- of the train." Do you recall that, sir? Can you find it?

utterances.speaker: SREDOJE SIMIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes. And he was very indignant about that and he was trying to explain to me that he had nothing to do with it.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: Not only was he indignant but would you say that he was upset, disturbed, angry about these defamatory and inaccurate statements?

utterances.speaker: SREDOJE SIMIC
utterances.text: Well, he really was. He even went pale, which was even more striking, as his hair was grey.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: I want you to look at the article that you have in front of you. And it's under the question that you asked Mr. Beara, "what really happened in Srebrenica in 1995"?

utterances.speaker: SREDOJE SIMIC
utterances.text: I found the passage.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: Going on down into that paragraph, or that answer about halfway, at least in the English translation, it said, "They had," meaning the ABiH army, "They had no real modern weapons." Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: SREDOJE SIMIC
utterances.text: It's not written that they hadn't had any modern weapons.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: Mr. Simic, could you just read that sentence or that is going to be different in English than it is in your text, in B/C/S, Serbian?

utterances.speaker: SREDOJE SIMIC
utterances.text: The answer says, "Srebrenica and Zepa were two separate enclaves under UN protection. Muslims were allegedly disarmed. In Crna Rijeka, there still exist weapons that they had turned over to the peacekeepers, but it's a scrap, old rifles, hand crafted, barely able to shoot. However, they did not turn over real modern weapons. In addition to UN peacekeepers or under the eyes of UN peacekeepers and observers, Muslims wreaked havoc. They left enclaves and attacked surrounding villages. In one place --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreter didn't hear the name of the place.

utterances.speaker: SREDOJE SIMIC
utterances.text: -- They killed everything and everyone.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: It's Pelemisi, for the interpreter, P-e-l-e-m-i-s-i.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: Sir, just for the record, then, Mr. Beara told you that, meaning the Muslims and the ABiH army, that they had -- "they did not turn over their real modern weapons, not that they did not have any real modern weapons," am I correct, sir?

utterances.speaker: SREDOJE SIMIC
utterances.text: From this answer it follows that they had modern weaponry but they surrendered old, obsolete weapons.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: Now, as far as speaking personally with Mr. Beara, can you tell me and tell the Trial Chamber what sort of dialect he had, if any, that you noticed, during the interview, when you spoke with him?

utterances.speaker: SREDOJE SIMIC
utterances.text: He spoke CroatSerbian, which is a mixture of Serbian and Bosnian-- Croatian and Bosnian, rather, with Dalmatian dialect. He had lived for a long time in Split n Dalmatia. I believe he mentioned that during the interview, so no wonder.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: Now, just a couple more questions, Mr. Simic, and I think we will be finished. Even though -- you've talked about why you went to speak with Mr. Beara, but would you agree that throughout this interview and the article you wrote from the interview, that Mr. Beara would speak about Srebrenica and Zepa?

utterances.speaker: SREDOJE SIMIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: All right. In fact, Zepa was mentioned again and again and again when Mr. Beara would talk about Srebrenica, even though you were only interested primarily in Srebrenica?

utterances.speaker: SREDOJE SIMIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: Now, so once you did the interview -- and by the way, the earlier -- maybe it's a translation error. You earlier said that the date of the article was 20 October 2002. Is that correct? Or was it the 29th of October 2002?

utterances.speaker: SREDOJE SIMIC
utterances.text: It's dated 29 October.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: Thank you. So when you got finished and you thought you had completed the article so that it was ready to go to print, you as a reporter, what did you do, sir? Who did you talk to?

utterances.speaker: SREDOJE SIMIC
utterances.text: To the editor-in-chief, who approved the article.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: And is that a normal thing that a reporter would go to the editor, let the editor read it for any changes, to see if would be printed or not printed and that sort of thing?

utterances.speaker: SREDOJE SIMIC
utterances.text: First of all, my editor-in-chief had approved that interview in advance. He approved the conditions set by Mr. Beara for the interview to take place at all. The usual practice is that the editor-in-chief on duty, in charge of that issue, and every issue has its own editor, prepares all the pages, all the articles that go into that issue, and could be sensitive, and he has to look at the articles first.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Simic. Did the -- did you have any discussions with the editor in regards to the content of the article that was about to go to press?

utterances.speaker: SREDOJE SIMIC
utterances.text: I can't remember, but I know that he told me as I was going to make the interview, to focus on the indictment and on Srebrenica, because that's what we were interested in. I remember -- yes, yes. I remember him saying to me to keep the tape, to keep the tape of that interview.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: Mr. Simic, you've been a reporter for a very long time, correct?

utterances.speaker: SREDOJE SIMIC
utterances.text: Well, rather a long time.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: And you've interviewed hundreds if not thousands of people for articles, would that be a fair statement?

utterances.speaker: SREDOJE SIMIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: From politicians, correct?

utterances.speaker: SREDOJE SIMIC
utterances.text: Politicians and ranking military men as well as businessmen.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: As a journalist, Mr. Simic, do you have any ethical obligations to not print something that you know is patently false?

utterances.speaker: SREDOJE SIMIC
utterances.text: Of course. Printing lies is against the law in Serbia, against all laws prevalent in the democratic world, everywhere in the world. When we are preparing texts and dealing with certain issues, we always try to hear both sides, and it often happens with young journalists who do not manage to get to the other side to have their articles refused. Their stories are not printed. For instance, when you give me an interview, there is no other side of the story. That's another possibility, when you are making an interview in which there is no other side, the assumption is that you believe the party giving the interview and you are as well prepared as you possibly can prepare.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: Thank you, sir. You just mentioned that at times, with, say, young journalists their articles are refused or not published or not printed, correct?

utterances.speaker: SREDOJE SIMIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: Isn't that the editor's final decision?

utterances.speaker: SREDOJE SIMIC
utterances.text: Of course, of course it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: And before the editor would publish a paper, wouldn't he talk to the reporter and ask the reporter, "Well, what do you think about this? What do you think about this article?" And did that happen with this article, sir?

utterances.speaker: SREDOJE SIMIC
utterances.text: Young journalists, young reporters, are talked to before and after the publishing. Their attention is drawn to certain matters before they go out to make a story, they are told what to focus on and after the story is written, somebody talks to them to point out any mistakes or something that was not quite professionally written. I have a good standing in my paper, and I don't necessarily get that treatment, but he -- I still wanted to talk to the editor, and he told me not to go into it too broadly, to focus on the indictment of the ICTY and the Srebrenica case, and to elicit the views and position of Mr. Beara on all that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Simic. And also, didn't the editor ask you before it went to final publication what your thoughts are about -- what your thoughts were and impressions of Mr. Beara's demeanour in answering the questions?

utterances.speaker: SREDOJE SIMIC
utterances.text: We didn't talk after the interview. That's why he told me to keep the tape, and I'm now sorry I didn't keep it. I probably wouldn't have to be here today and I would have facilitated the work of the Trial Chamber and probably have made it easier for Mr. Beara himself. But I told him about my impressions. I can't really call them opinions, just impressions, that I got during the interview.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: Would you share those impressions with the Trial Chamber, sir?

utterances.speaker: SREDOJE SIMIC
utterances.text: I don't know if it is really relevant. I had the impression that at that critical moment, Mr. Beara hadn't really been there, around Srebrenica. That was the feeling I came away with. I had talked to many people. I had interviewed hard-core criminals before. And you get a feeling that enables to you distinguish when somebody is spinning a yarn and somebody who is really opening their soul to you and telling you the truth. And I told my editor that because of all that, I have a feeling that Mr. Beara was not going to surrender. That was my feeling then. But I'm -- I am now glad that he didn't take an alternative course.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: Your opinion and impression was that Ljubisa Beara told you the truth, correct?

utterances.speaker: SREDOJE SIMIC
utterances.text: Well, yes, but even if he hadn't -- or rather, if I had the impression he wasn't telling me the truth, I would still have published the interview because it is not up to me. I don't have the right to doubt, second guess what he's saying.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: Correct. I agree with that, sir. One more question. Mr. Simic, if you had felt that or had the impression that he wasn't telling you the truth during that interview, you would certainly tell the Trial Chamber that today under oath, would you not?

utterances.speaker: SREDOJE SIMIC
utterances.text: Of course I would. Like I said everything else.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: And one final question, and it just comes up on your last answer that you are glad now that Ljubisa Beara didn't take an alternative course, I'm not quite sure what you mean by that but I think you recall, you asked him in the interview if he would take a gun and start shooting if he were to be arrested. Do you recall that question?

utterances.speaker: SREDOJE SIMIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: And do you recall the answer, sir?

utterances.speaker: SREDOJE SIMIC
utterances.text: No, I don't.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: I'm going to read the answer and tell me if it will refresh your recollection. "Will you use force to defend yourself," the question you asked Mr. Beara. And his answer to you was, "No. I won't shoot. These are our children. They are doing their job." Do you recall that, sir?

utterances.speaker: SREDOJE SIMIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: Thank you very much. I have no further questions, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Nicholls, do you have redirect?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Just briefly, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Go ahead.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: If I could --

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Sir, I want to go back to one of these soul bearing answers that Mr. Beara gave you and Mr. -- my friend, Mr. Meek read out part of it, and this was to the question and it's on page 2 of the interview. It's the last question, I think, in column 3. The question was: "Are you trying to say that the VRS did not commit mass crimes in Srebrenica?" And the part that was read out to you by Mr. Meek was, "What nonsense, it's not possible to carry out killings on such a mass scale in the presence of UN representatives, even if one had such an insane idea." In the text it goes on, his answer continues: "In order to kill so many people in such a short time, one would need to engage a brigade. I know that sooner or later the truth on Srebrenica will come to the surface, just as we don't know what happened in Markale, everyone knew that the Muslims killed their own people in order to accuse the Serbs so that NATO could launch air strikes against us because of crimes against civilians. I'm convinced that Markale is a mini-Srebrenica and a mini-Zepa." Then you follow this up with a question which is in the next column, "Does it mean that Srebrenica was in fact engineered by the Muslims for propaganda purposes," and Mr. Beara answered, "I'm convinced it was. I don't know what the reason was, but it is monstrous to kill one's own people in order to spite someone." That's exactly what they did in Markale and the bread queues in Sarajevo" --

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'm just going to object because this article is going to come in. If he wants to read the whole thing out to the Court. I don't know what the purpose is.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: We haven't had the question as yet.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: I know. That's my point, Judge.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yeah, yeah, but let him come with the question, because I can anticipate the question and I think you will sit down after that. Yes, Mr. Nicholls.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: That's exactly what they did in Markale and the bread queue in Sarajevo. They killed their own innocent civilians so that we would be blamed so that the Serbs would be presented as criminals to the world. And he goes on to say how only Alija Izetbegovic and his fanatics could come up with such a plan. Now, is that correct? Is that the full answer to the question Mr. Meek's brought to you, that it was nonsense about the killings in Sarajevo -- in Srebrenica because the entire killings of the Muslims had been done by the Muslims themselves for propaganda? Is that what he told you was the truth?

utterances.speaker: SREDOJE SIMIC
utterances.text: He told me what I wrote down in the article. Actually, I'm afraid I didn't understand the gist of your question.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: I'm saying the article is correct, that is what Mr. Beara's full answer was to the nonsense of the crimes in Srebrenica.

utterances.speaker: SREDOJE SIMIC
utterances.text: As far as I could understand him while we were talking, while the interview was being conducted, he considered every crime a crime, irrespective who the perpetrator of that crime was. He also told me about the incident in Montenegro that he was angry about it, that this should not have happened, and that it would not have happened if people had more --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I think you're avoiding answering the question. The question was a very simple one. It's is this what essentially he told you as the truth, what has been read out to you by Mr. Nicholls?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] What Mr. Nicholls read out is what is written in the article, which means that this is what Mr. Beara said.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes?

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: I have a question, Judge, if you don't mind.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: If you address it to us first, please?

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: Yes. May I please have one question to clear something up?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Just let us know what the question is, and then we authorise it or don't authorise it.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: Okay. The question is with this last set of questions my friend Mr. Nicholls has I think misconstrued the witness's testimony. He earlier testified that after interviewing him, and he's interviewed hundreds, if not thousands of people, he had the feeling, the impression and opinion that Mr. Beara was telling the truth that he was not present when it happened and didn't come back until it was over with. Now, other things about Markale, the market and things like that are separate, obviously, and that's what I wanted to ask and clarify with the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. Go ahead. Further cross-examination by Mr. Meek:

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Mr. Simic, very briefly. Earlier when you were describing your feelings and opinions and impressions of Mr. Beara, didn't you in fact testify that you came away from that interview and meeting with Mr. Beara with a feeling that, in fact, he had not been present immediately before the Srebrenica action and didn't come back to that area until it was all over with, as he told you in the part of that interview?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Nicholls?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: I know you heard the question, but I really don't see how this arises out of my question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: It does arise. Let's proceed. Go ahead, Mr. Simic, if you could kindly answer that question?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. I've already told you that my impression was that Mr. Beara had not been at that location at that critical moment. But that was just my impression, nothing else.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. I thank you. Is there any of the Defence teams that wishes to -- no? Judge Kwon, Judge Prost? Mr. Simic, that brings your testimony to an end. You're free to go back home. You will be assisted by our staff. On behalf of the Trial Chamber I wish to thank you for having come over to give testimony and also wish you a safe journey back home.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Mr. Nicholls, documents? May I, before we do this, I take it there is not going to be another witness today. I got the feeling that was the agreement yesterday.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: That is correct. That's the way we would like to proceed, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. Then can I ask for the indulgence of everyone to proceed until we finish, which shouldn't take us long, and rather than have a break? Except that I have -- yes, Mr. Ostojic.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Mr. President, I'm not sure but we have a couple of issues we'd like to clear up --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yeah, yeah.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: -- with the Court so we need time after the documents to discuss it. We need some guidance on a prior order, among other issues, if the Court permits, we'd like to have five, ten minutes to do that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. Then I think we will need to have a break. We will have the usual break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: So we'll have a 15-minute break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Let's start with documents first. Where is Mr. Nicholls? Here he is.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Sorry, Your Honours. The only document is 480, the newspaper article.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you. Any objection?

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: No objection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you. No objection, I suppose, from the other Defence teams. It is so admitted. Yes. Now I understand that some of you wish to address the Chamber. Mr. Bourgon, earlier on you had indicated that you wished to address the Chamber.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Won't be necessary, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. I thank you and I appreciate that very much, Mr. Bourgon. And Mr. Ostojic?

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. I did have two points but I'd like first, we had some documents to tender to the Court as well, if we may, and that would have been the information report from the OTP dated the 16th of December 2005, as well as, although I don't think it was covered so in any detail if very little, was the statement provided to the Belgrade district court March 24th, 2006.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Any objection?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: No, Your Honour, definitely not to the information report. I'm not sure that the -- his prior testimony was covered at all or why it's necessary. But I don't object.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. Finished. All right. It's over. They are so admitted. They have both been translated, to my knowledge. One is in English in any case.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: One is in English --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yeah.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: -- and has been translated and the other one I understand has also been translated from B/C/S to English because we have that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you. They are so admitted and they will be numbered by --

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: I can give you the numbers, Your Honour. It was 2D127 for the December 16th, 2005 exhibit and 2D128 for the Belgrade district court statement of March 24th, 2006.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. I thank you so much, Mr. Ostojic. You wish to address the Chamber on something else?

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Yes. On a housekeeping matter we are looking for some guidance from the Trial Chamber in connection with the intercept briefings that we are all working on. The Court's prior order indicated that the deadline, and we were grateful for the additional week extension, to be filed on the 18th of June, but in reading the order and our discussions in court, it was always envisioned at least from my view that the deadline would be set upon the conclusion of Mr. Rodic's testimony and unfortunately that testimony was not concluded last week, not to blame the OTP on it, but we did have some difficulties with lengthy witnesses at that time. So we're looking for guidance from the Court as to what exactly is the firm deadline so that some of us don't file it and others read into the order suggesting that it's after. We also, just for the Court's information, are working with Mr. Rodic closely, or Mr. Zivanovic is, and we can confirm we think by Monday exactly when he can testify and we are obviously blocking out the dates of two critical witnesses that the OTP has who were -- plead guilty and are coming from other countries. We are not interfering with those dates that they've set in stone, so we will work around that. We hope to get him here before the 20th of June sometime before that in order to conclude his cross and redirect examination.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I quite understand the point that you have made, but just as food for thought more than anything else for the time being, because obviously this is something that we will need to discuss privately, or in Chambers, wouldn't you also consider the possibility of sticking to the date that we had set before, that is I forgot exactly.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: 18th of June, I believe, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: 18th of June, as being the deadline with the understanding that anything that comes -- that emerges from his further testimony would entitle you automatically to file further submissions because by now --

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: We are working on it obviously. We are not looking for an extended delay, but to the extent that something may arise, we thought if a week after his testimony which shouldn't take us more than I believe the 25th of June, quite candidly, because we hope to get him in before the 20th of June in those --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I think we can tell you here and now with the understanding that we are not consulting Judge Stole on this, because he's not here, but ultimately it's us who decide. Here and now we would meet you on that. So we can extend it orally to the 25th, if there is need to extend it further by one day, two days, I don't think it's going to make a difference.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President and Your Honours. We are very grateful for that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: And thank you, Mr. Ostojic, for raising it because it was in our mind. We didn't know exactly when he was coming back and obviously we, at least speaking for myself, I was anticipating something like this kind of submission, although we have not discussed it amongst ourselves. Yes, thank you so much.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: And my second issue, if I may proceed, Your Honour --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, of course.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: -- is it involves early in the trial the Court was given and the Prosecutor estimated what the length of their case was and the Court had informed OLAD what they thought the case would be from the OTP standpoint, and I'm a little embarrassed to bring the issue up but it's very critical for all our members of the Defence team and the people who assist us, and that's our budgetary concerns. The Court had indicated at that time in August I believe that there was an 11-and-a-half-month period that they felt the Prosecution may complete their case and I think we have been working at a reasonable good pace. And the issue has come up in other cases and OLAD has essentially generally told us that the Trial Chamber has to convey a message if they think it should be extended because of the breaks that are involved. We're bringing it to the Court's attention, if you don't mind respectfully, to keep it in mind, and if you would like our input on that, we're prepared to discuss it. Obviously, we need the input of the Prosecutor. There are other developments that the Prosecutor would like, I'm sure, to discuss with the Court or from my understanding they would. So it may change but we definitely think it's an important issue because we're coming up to that 10th month and so period.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. We consider it very important too and I can assure you we have been studying it and discussing it amongst ourselves and I would anticipate that very shortly we'll come with our ruling on that matter when the Prosecution is expected to finish their case. But I thank you for raising it.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: But I want to put your mind at rest, all of you, that this is on our discussion table and we have been going through it. Yes, thank you, Mr. Ostojic.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Mr. McCloskey? I think I can anticipate also what you are about to say.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: I have supported and I continue to support the Defence's financial issues with OLAD, though I'm not sure I'm a party to it but I can support them in that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: We are not a party to it too, but we have intermittently also given our support without you even knowing.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Could we go into private session?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Of course, Mr. McCloskey. Let's go into private session, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We are back in open session, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, we are in open session. Mr. Bourgon.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. There is one issue I would like to bring at this time to the Court's attention on behalf of all Defence teams. (redacted)

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: One moment. One moment. And I'm sorry I'm interrupting you like this. Let's go back into private session for a short while, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: On Tuesday of this week when you were dealing with the --

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We are in open session, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: I'm grateful. On Tuesday of this week when you were dealing with the tendering into evidence of documents relating to witness 109, that's Trivic, there is no reason I shouldn't mention his name, Mr. Sarapa sought to tender into evidence two documents, 7D550 and 7D551, which you astutely observed had not been released into e-court. They now have. Can they now be tendered into evidence, please?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you. There was no objection to tendering --

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: No, there wasn't.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: -- at the time, although I am under the impression that one of them had already been tendered by someone else.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: I think it's highly unlikely. They were short passages of witness interviews that we had tailored particularly for that cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: In any case, they are so admitted.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: No other interventions? Which brings this sitting to an end. As you know, we entertained your request to have a short break in order to be able to reorganise a little bit your ranks, which is badly needed. We have been working hard, incessantly, and we are al somewhat tired. I think the first part of this morning's sitting was revealing. It suggest that you drink less coffee and more Camomile. I think that could be a solution. But, anyway, you know when we will reconvene. Please have a rest while we are not sitting in the course of next week, and then the week after, I suppose we will have all sorts of problems starting with what Mr. McCloskey has referred to and possibly anticipated and also the motion that we are expecting today. Thank you. You know that on the 11th, we are not sitting because initially Mr. Meek had asked for the 11th, too, and we had turned his request down and then we've agreed that it was a well-deserved request, so we acceded to it as well. All right. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: to be reconvened on Tuesday, the 12th day of June, 2007, at 9.00. 19 20 21 22 23 24 25
